record.paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
record.original_question: How can observations of particles with energies above 60 × 10^18 electron-volts be reconciled with the standard interpretation of the cosmic microwave background radiation, given that interactions with microwave-background photons impose a theoretical propagation limit for particles traveling more than about 20 to 50 megaparsecs?

evidence.quote: For example, many particles are seen with energies over 60 × 1018 eV. But that is the theoretical energy limit for anything traveling for more than 20-50 Mpc because of interaction with microwave background photons[161]. This is a problem for the actual interpretation of CMBR in the Big Bang theory.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Cosmic-ray primaries arriving at Earth are observed with energies exceeding $E_{\rm GZK} \approx 6\times 10^{19}$ eV. According to the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) argument, an ultra-high-energy proton (or nucleus) propagating through an isotropic blackbody radiation field at temperature $T \approx 2.725$ K (the cosmic microwave background, CMB) loses energy by photopion production $p + \gamma_{\rm CMB} \to p + \pi^0$ (or $\to n + \pi^+$), and analogous photodisintegration processes for nuclei. The energy-loss length for protons above this threshold is of order $20$–$50$ Mpc, so that any such primary originating at cosmological distances should be degraded below the threshold before reaching Earth.

Assuming
(i) the standard cosmological interpretation of the CMB as a relic blackbody bath filling all of space at $T \approx 2.725$ K,
(ii) standard-model particle physics governing the proton–photon (and nucleus–photon) cross sections, and
(iii) sources of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays distributed predominantly at extragalactic distances $\gg 50$ Mpc,

provide a quantitative, self-consistent mechanism that reconciles the observed flux of cosmic-ray events with energies above $6\times 10^{19}$ eV with the GZK propagation bound. A satisfactory answer should either:
(a) identify and characterize a population of sources within the GZK horizon ($\lesssim 100$ Mpc) capable of producing the observed integral flux, arrival-direction distribution, and mass composition; or
(b) specify modifications of propagation physics (e.g., new particles, Lorentz-invariance violation, or modified dispersion relations) that suppress the energy losses, while remaining consistent with all other CMB-related observations.
artifact.category_tag: Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and the GZK cutoff
artifact.status_search_result: The expected flux suppression near the GZK energy has been confirmed at high significance by the Pierre Auger Observatory, HiRes, and Telescope Array, so the existence of events above the threshold is no longer in tension with the CMB interpretation per se. However, whether the observed suppression is fully due to the GZK effect or partly reflects the maximum acceleration energy at sources remains unsettled, and the mass composition reported by Auger (heavier) versus Telescope Array (lighter) is still under active debate. The problem of identifying the nearby sources of trans-GZK events is therefore only partially resolved.

status_evidence.title: Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin limit - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: A suppression of the cosmic-ray flux that can be explained with the GZK limit has been confirmed... the Pierre Auger Observatory effect is statistically significant at the level of 20 standard deviations.
status_evidence.claim: Observed flux suppression near the GZK energy is confirmed, reconciling observations with standard CMB physics.

status_evidence.title: Ultra High Energy Cosmic Rays: A Short Review - Aloisio
status_evidence.snippet: HiRes and Telescope Array results are compatible with a light (proton) composition while Auger indicates heavier composition; it remains controversial whether the suppression is due to GZK.
status_evidence.claim: The interpretation of the suppression and the composition above the GZK energy is still debated.
